summary: Asks whether high post-2020 macro uncertainty will persist. Uses the JLN macro uncertainty index (AR(1) persistence, Fed trade-off months, market-vs-forecast disagreement) and decade asset performance. Concludes uncertainty will likely stay high and investors should diversify via bonds, commodities, risk parity, trend following and macro.

coverage.note: JLN index definition, history, JLN>1 equity results, footnotes 1-3
AR(1) persistence, current level and forecasts, two catalysts, transmission
Friedman lags, trade-off months test, wealth effect, disagreement
futures vs SEP, breakevens vs consensus, footnotes 7-10
cross-asset disagreement, JLN vs VIX, SVB footnote 11
decade Sharpe ratios, risk parity, data definitions
trend following in drawdowns, macro, diversification advice
nothing actionable: reference list (citations captured where used)
legal disclosures summarised; AQR fund in SG Trend index

claims.speaker: Jordan Brooks
claims.quote: macreconomic uncertainty is currently high versus history when measured quantitatively
claims.claim: Macroeconomic uncertainty as of mid-2023 is high relative to its own history when measured with a quantitative index.
claims.testable: yes - compare current JLN to its history

claims.speaker: Jordan Brooks
claims.quote: We can quantify macroeconomic uncertainty by measuring the degree to which the economy has become more or less predictable over time.
claims.claim: Macro uncertainty is measured as the (un)predictability of economic data: small prediction errors mean low uncertainty, large errors mean high uncertainty.
claims.exact_rule: uncertainty_t = size/volatility of forecast errors of macro data releases at t (high errors -> high uncertainty)
claims.data_needed: macro data releases and their forecasts

claims.speaker: Jordan Brooks
claims.quote: banking sector is beginning to reel from compressed margins (which show up today as losses if marked to market, and tomorrow as lower earnings) and a shrinking deposit base
claims.claim: Rate hikes compress bank margins, which appear as mark-to-market losses now and lower earnings later, while deposits shrink.
claims.testable: partly - bank NIM and deposit data are observable

claims.speaker: Jordan Brooks
claims.quote: use a large set of economic releases to build a comprehensive monthly “macro uncertainty index.”
claims.claim: The JLN index summarises uncertainty across a large set of economic releases into one monthly number.
claims.data_needed: JLN macro uncertainty index (Jurado, Ludvigson, Ng 2015), monthly, from Sydney Ludvigson website

claims.speaker: Jordan Brooks
claims.quote: The authors use a high-dimensional statistical factor model to produce one-month-ahead forecasts of 132 macroeconomic series.
claims.claim: JLN forecasts 132 macro series one month ahead with a high-dimensional factor model; its forecast errors are the raw material of the index.
claims.exact_rule: Factor-model one-month-ahead forecasts of 132 US macro series; take forecast errors
claims.data_needed: 132 US monthly macroeconomic series (JLN data set)

claims.speaker: Jordan Brooks
claims.quote: The uncertainty index is the common component of the conditional volatility of the forecast errors at each point in time.
claims.claim: The index is the common factor of the conditional volatilities of the 132 forecast errors, standardized to mean 0, sd 1.
claims.exact_rule: Index_t = common component of conditional volatility of forecast errors across 132 series; z-score (mean 0, sd 1)
claims.data_needed: JLN macro uncertainty index (Jurado, Ludvigson, Ng 2015), monthly, from Sydney Ludvigson website

claims.speaker: Jordan Brooks
claims.quote: taking the absolute value of the difference between actual and forecasted values for year-on-year real GDP growth, CPI inflation, and industrial production growth
claims.claim: A simple cross-check uncertainty measure is the quarterly average absolute forecast error of y/y real GDP growth, CPI inflation and industrial production growth.
claims.exact_rule: Simple index_q = mean over {real GDP y/y, CPI y/y, IP y/y} of |actual - forecast|, each quarter
claims.data_needed: Actuals and forecasts (source unstated) of US real GDP y/y, CPI y/y, IP y/y, quarterly
claims.testable: yes - forecast and actual data available

claims.speaker: Jordan Brooks
claims.quote: By virtue of equating uncertainty to the conditional volatility of forecast errors, as opposed to the magnitude of realized forecast errors, JLN is more theoretically appealing.
claims.claim: The author prefers JLN because it measures expected (conditional) volatility of forecast errors rather than realized errors, and uses many more series.

claims.speaker: Jordan Brooks
claims.quote: Nevertheless, the two indices track each other well, with a correlation 0.7.
claims.claim: The simple realized-forecast-error index and JLN are 0.7 correlated, supporting the reasonableness of JLN.
claims.reported_result: Correlation JLN vs simple 3-series forecast-error index = 0.7 (sample not stated, quarterly)

claims.speaker: Jordan Brooks
claims.quote: It peaked in the first half of 2020 and is currently at levels not seen since the 1980s, save for during the global financial crisis.
claims.claim: JLN peaked in H1 2020 and at end-2022 sits at levels last seen in the 1980s apart from the GFC.
claims.reported_result: Figure 1 (Jul 1960-Dec 2022, z-score; read from chart): 2020 peak ~5.3, GFC 2008-09 peak ~4.1, early-1980s peak ~3.0, mid-1970s ~2.2; end-2022 ~1.3

claims.speaker: Jordan Brooks
claims.quote: a decade during which macro uncertainty was consistently, and often meaningfully, below average.
claims.claim: The 2010s were a decade of consistently below-average macro uncertainty, in contrast to the 2020s.
claims.reported_result: Figure 1: JLN mostly between about -1.0 and 0 during 2010-2019 (read from chart)

claims.speaker: Jordan Brooks
claims.quote: During months in which the JLN index exceeds one, average annualized excess returns for U.S. equities is -16 percent and average annualized realized volatility is 21 percent
claims.claim: When JLN > 1, US equities have averaged -16% annualized excess return and 21% realized vol, versus +6% and 12% in other months.
claims.exact_rule: Condition: JLN_t > 1 (z-score); compare same-month US equity excess return and realized vol vs other months
claims.data_needed: JLN monthly; US equity excess returns and realized volatility (index unstated), 1960-2022 implied
claims.reported_result: JLN>1 months: US equity excess return -16% ann., realized vol 21% ann.; other months +6% and 12% (contemporaneous, gross, sample ~1960-2022)
claims.direction: equities down, vol up when JLN > 1

claims.speaker: Jordan Brooks
claims.quote: Historically, macro uncertainty tends to be very persistent—on the scale of quarters and years, not weeks and
claims.claim: Macro uncertainty is highly persistent, with high and low uncertainty periods clustering for quarters to years.

claims.speaker: Jordan Brooks
claims.quote: the current monetary policy and market backdrop strongly supports the premise uncertainty is here to stay.
claims.claim: Beyond statistics, the current policy and market backdrop supports the view that uncertainty stays high.
claims.testable: partly - forecast can be checked ex post

claims.speaker: Jordan Brooks
claims.quote: This note discusses the drivers of subdued macroeconomic volatility during the 2010s, and links it to the below average performance of trend following strategies during that decade.
claims.claim: A referenced AQR note links low macro volatility in the 2010s to below-average trend-following returns in that decade.
claims.direction: low macro uncertainty -> weaker trend following
claims.testable: yes - regress trend returns on macro vol

claims.speaker: Jordan Brooks
claims.quote: asset returns are notoriously difficult to forecast, asset volatility tends to be persistent and, therefore, much more predictable
claims.claim: Volatility, unlike returns, is persistent and therefore predictable; the author applies the same idea to macro uncertainty.

claims.speaker: Jordan Brooks
claims.claim: An AR(1) on monthly JLN gives a coefficient of 0.98 with R-squared 97%, so macro uncertainty is extremely persistent.
claims.exact_rule: OLS: JLN_{t+1} = b * JLN_t (no constant shown); b = 0.98; forecast h months ahead = b^h * JLN_t
claims.data_needed: JLN macro uncertainty index (Jurado, Ludvigson, Ng 2015), monthly, from Sydney Ludvigson website

claims.speaker: Jordan Brooks
claims.quote: The half- life of shocks to macro uncertainty is around 4 years.
claims.claim: Shocks to macro uncertainty have a half-life of about four years, and a value of 1.0 is expected to decay to about 0.8 a year later.
claims.reported_result: 0.98^12 ~ 0.8 after one year; half-life ~4 years (as stated)

claims.speaker: Jordan Brooks
claims.quote: stands at 1.27, which is the 88 percentile relative to history
claims.claim: At end-2022 JLN was 1.27, the 88th percentile of its history, though well below its highest spikes.

claims.speaker: Jordan Brooks
claims.quote: The one-year forecast is 1.06 (85 th percentile), and the two-year forecast is 0.89 (84 th percentile).
claims.claim: The AR(1) model forecasts JLN of 1.06 one year ahead and 0.89 two years ahead, both still well above average.
claims.reported_result: JLN forecast end-2023 = 1.06 (85th pct), end-2024 = 0.89 (84th pct)

claims.speaker: Jordan Brooks
claims.quote: Statistical forecasts are far from sure things.
claims.claim: The persistence-based forecast is uncertain and may be wrong if this time is different.

claims.speaker: Jordan Brooks
claims.quote: In this simple time series model the R 2 is simply the slope coefficient squared.
claims.claim: The 97% R-squared just restates the persistence (slope squared) and is not evidence of forecasting skill beyond persistence.

claims.speaker: Jordan Brooks
claims.quote: The impact of aggressive rate hikes is only starting to be felt, and central banks are facing tradeoffs between employment and inflation for the first time in decades.
claims.claim: Catalyst 1 for persistent uncertainty: lagged effects of aggressive hikes plus a new employment-inflation trade-off for central banks.
claims.testable: partly - trade-off months can be defined and tested

claims.speaker: Jordan Brooks
claims.quote: Market-implied expectations of key economic variables disagree materially with policymaker and economist forecasts, and even disagree across markets.
claims.claim: Catalyst 2: market pricing disagrees with official and economist forecasts and across markets, which must resolve via volatility.

claims.speaker: Jordan Brooks
claims.quote: Monetary policy influences economic activity primarily through its impact on interest rate-sensitive components of demand
claims.claim: Monetary policy works mainly through rate-sensitive demand such as business and housing investment and consumer durables, with lags.
claims.testable: partly - standard macro, lag length variable

claims.speaker: Jordan Brooks
claims.quote: higher interest rates and a flattening yield curve typically compressing net interest margins, leading banks to reduce the availability of credit.
claims.claim: Higher rates and a flatter curve compress bank net interest margins, so banks cut credit supply, which slows the economy with a lag.
claims.indicator: yield curve slope; bank NIM; credit availability
claims.testable: partly - bank lending surveys and NIM data

claims.speaker: Milton Friedman (cited by author)
claims.quote: monetary actions affect economic conditions only after a lag that is both long and variable.
claims.claim: Citing Milton Friedman, monetary policy affects the economy with long and variable lags, so the 2022 hikes have not yet fully hit.

claims.speaker: Jordan Brooks
claims.quote: the impact of changes in liquid asset wealth on consumption is pennies on the dollar
claims.claim: Fast asset-price reactions do not mean fast transmission, because the wealth effect on consumption is small and concentrated among wealthy households.

claims.speaker: Jordan Brooks
claims.quote: when inflation was running hot, economic activity was typically quite strong; when inflation was languishing below target, economic activity was typically weak.
claims.claim: For decades inflation and activity moved together, so policy direction was unambiguous; that alignment has now broken.
claims.testable: yes - correlation of inflation and activity gaps by era

claims.speaker: Jordan Brooks
claims.quote: All central banks, de facto if not de jure, strive for full employment and low inflation.
claims.claim: Even single-mandate central banks such as the ECB effectively care about employment, so the trade-off logic applies globally.

claims.speaker: Jordan Brooks
claims.quote: Historically, central banks facing tradeoffs has been a catalyst for elevated macro uncertainty.
claims.claim: When central banks face a trade-off between inflation and employment, macro uncertainty rises because policy can change abruptly and its path is unclear.
claims.testable: yes - tested with trade-off months below

claims.speaker: Jordan Brooks
claims.quote: the Volcker Fed cut interest rates in 1980 when unemployment rose, only to begin a hiking cycle shortly thereafter inducing a prolonged recession.
claims.claim: Example: in 1980 the Volcker Fed cut then re-hiked, showing how trade-offs produce abrupt policy reversals.

claims.speaker: Jordan Brooks
claims.quote: note the enormous volatility at the front end of the yield curve in March 2023 as a case-in-point
claims.claim: Example: front-end yield volatility in March 2023, when banking concerns caused sharp downward revisions to policy expectations.

claims.speaker: Jordan Brooks
claims.quote: defined as months in which core PCE inflation exceeded four percent (twice the Fed’s target) and unemployment was above the Congressional Budget Office estimate of NAIRU
claims.claim: Trade-off months are defined as months with core PCE inflation above 4% and unemployment above the CBO NAIRU estimate.
claims.exact_rule: Tradeoff_t = 1 if core PCE inflation y/y > 4% AND unemployment rate > CBO NAIRU estimate; else 0
claims.data_needed: US core PCE inflation (BEA), unemployment rate (BLS), CBO NAIRU / noncyclical rate of unemployment
claims.testable: yes - simple dummy from public data

claims.speaker: Jordan Brooks
claims.quote: JLN averaged 0.6 vs. -0.1 in all other months.
claims.claim: In trade-off months JLN averaged 0.6 versus -0.1 otherwise, so policy trade-offs coincide with above-average macro uncertainty.
claims.reported_result: Mean JLN: trade-off months 0.6 vs other months -0.1 (sample ~1960-2022)

claims.speaker: Jordan Brooks
claims.quote: the difference- in-means is highly significant, with a t-stat in excess of seven.
claims.claim: The difference in JLN between trade-off and other months is statistically significant (t > 7).
claims.reported_result: t-stat > 7 for difference in means (no adjustment for JLN autocorrelation stated)

claims.speaker: Jordan Brooks
claims.quote: markets and policymaker and economist forecasts disagree on the evolution of key macroeconomic variables: interest rates, inflation, and growth.
claims.claim: Disagreement between market prices and official/economist forecasts on rates, inflation and growth is a second catalyst for sustained uncertainty.

claims.speaker: Jordan Brooks
claims.quote: The futures market is currently pricing the May 3 rate hike was the final of this cycle.
claims.claim: As of May 2023 fed funds futures priced the May hike as the last, with cuts from September 2023.
claims.reported_result: May 3 2023 futures: last hike May 2023; cuts begin Sep 2023 (Figure 2 LHS)

claims.speaker: Jordan Brooks
claims.quote: At the beginning of March, it was pricing a peak funds rate of nearly 6 percent, and a funds rate of 4.25 percent at the end of 2024.
claims.claim: Futures pricing swung hugely within two months: early March priced a ~6% peak and 4.25% end-2024, May priced ~3% end-2024 after ~2.25% of cuts.
claims.reported_result: Figure 2 LHS (read from chart): Mar 8 2023 curve peak ~5.65% mid-2023, ~4.1-4.4% 2024-26; Jan 18 curve peak ~4.9%; May 3 curve ~5.1% falling to ~2.75% by 2025; SEP diamonds ~5.1% (2023), ~4.1% (2024), ~3.1% (2025)

claims.speaker: Jordan Brooks
claims.quote: Volatility at the front end of the curve is indicative of elevated economic uncertainty.
claims.claim: Large swings in front-end rate pricing are a market sign of high economic uncertainty.

claims.speaker: Jordan Brooks
claims.quote: The disparity between FOMC projections and futures market pricing is the largest observed since the SEP began in 2012.
claims.claim: The gap between FOMC dot projections and futures pricing (FOMC and >70% of FT economists saw zero 2023 cuts) was the largest since the SEP began in 2012.
claims.reported_result: Largest SEP-vs-futures gap since 2012 (as of Mar/May 2023); >70% of FT-surveyed economists forecast zero cuts in 2023 (FT, Mar 19 2023)
claims.indicator: FOMC SEP fed funds median minus futures-implied rate

claims.speaker: Jordan Brooks
claims.quote: Either scenario is likely to contribute to financial market volatility and continued elevated macro uncertainty.
claims.claim: Disagreement must resolve either by repricing rate expectations or by eroding Fed credibility; both raise volatility and uncertainty.
claims.testable: partly - test whether SEP-futures gap predicts rate volatility

claims.speaker: Jordan Brooks
claims.quote: Inflation-linked bond markets forecast inflation returning to two percent over the next year and staying there for the next decade.
claims.claim: Breakevens priced ~2% inflation from year one, while consensus forecasts saw slower disinflation from ~4%.
claims.reported_result: Figure 2 RHS (as of Apr 11/May 3 2023, read from chart): realized y/y inflation 5.0%; consensus 1Y ~3.9%, 2Y ~3.2%, 3Y ~2.9%, ~2.5% by 10Y; breakevens ~2.0-2.2% flat 1Y-10Y
claims.indicator: inflation breakevens vs Consensus Economics forecasts

claims.speaker: Jordan Brooks
claims.quote: This is not the first time this hiking cycle futures markets have dramatically piled on bets of lower rates.
claims.claim: Futures also priced early cuts after June 2022 and autumn 2022 data, then reversed, so such rallies have repeatedly proved premature in this cycle.

claims.speaker: Jordan Brooks
claims.quote: The difference between the futures market-implied path of the funds rate and surveys may be partially explained by a negative risk premium in futures pricing.
claims.claim: Part of the futures-survey gap may be a negative term premium: investors pay to hold long futures as insurance against a recession with lower rates.
claims.direction: futures-implied path biased low vs expected path
claims.testable: partly - compare futures to realized rates

claims.speaker: Jordan Brooks
claims.quote: a de-anchoring of long-term inflation expectations would make disinflation much more challenging, likely requiring a steeper cost in terms of economic weakness and unemployment.
claims.claim: If long-run inflation expectations de-anchor, disinflation would require more unemployment because expectations drive actual inflation.
claims.conditions: if core inflation stays above target or re-emerges after a pivot

claims.speaker: Jordan Brooks
claims.quote: a de-anchoring could prompt nominal bondholders to demand a significant inflation risk premium as in the 1980s.
claims.claim: De-anchored inflation expectations would push up the inflation risk premium in nominal bond yields, as in the 1980s (Brooks 2021; Ilmanen 2011 ch. 9).

claims.speaker: Jordan Brooks
claims.quote: But a deep recession would be very painful for equities, which show no evidence of pricing in a slowdown.
claims.claim: Rate and inflation markets may be pricing a sharp slowdown, but equities are not, so asset classes disagree with each other.

claims.speaker: Jordan Brooks
claims.quote: the large amount of disagreement indicates that the economy is on a knife’s edge, and dissonant market pricing is a powder keg for higher volatility.
claims.claim: Large disagreement between and across markets and forecasters signals a fragile economy and sets up higher volatility.

claims.speaker: Jordan Brooks
claims.quote: I am not arguing policymakers and economists have it right and markets wrong, or vice versa.
claims.claim: The author takes no view on who is right; the argument is only that disagreement implies volatility.

claims.speaker: Jordan Brooks
claims.quote: Figure 3 plots JLN against 22-day realized equity market volatility and the VIX index (all series standardized).
claims.claim: Macro uncertainty is compared to standardized 22-day realized equity volatility and the VIX.
claims.exact_rule: z-score JLN, 22-day realized equity vol, VIX; compare/correlate
claims.data_needed: JLN; US equity daily returns (22-day realized vol); VIX (Cboe)

claims.speaker: Jordan Brooks
claims.quote: JLN is 0.6 correlated with VIX and 0.5 correlated with realized volatility.
claims.claim: Macro uncertainty co-moves with market volatility (corr 0.6 with VIX, 0.5 with realized vol), so persistent uncertainty implies persistent high market vol.
claims.reported_result: corr(JLN, VIX) = 0.6; corr(JLN, 22-day realized vol) = 0.5 (Figure 3, ~1965-2022; z-scores, spikes to ~9 in 2008 and ~8 in 2020)

claims.speaker: Jordan Brooks
claims.quote: systemic bank failures and financial crises have typically been the result of deteriorating asset quality on bank balance sheets, not the composition of their deposits or duration mismatches.
claims.claim: The author judges SVB/Signature unlikely to spark a systemic crisis because crises usually stem from asset-quality deterioration, not deposit mix or duration mismatch.

claims.speaker: Jordan Brooks
claims.quote: since the end of February, real GDP growth forecasts were revised up by an average of 40 basis points, according to data from Consensus Economics.
claims.claim: Forecasters raised real GDP growth forecasts by 40bp after end-February 2023, showing little expectation of an imminent calamity.
claims.reported_result: Consensus Economics real GDP forecasts +40bp on average since end-Feb 2023

claims.speaker: Jordan Brooks
claims.quote: the level of uncertainty at the front end of the yield curve led the Silicon Valley Bank shock to cause to a massive re-pricing of monetary policy expectations
claims.claim: Because front-end uncertainty was already high, a modest shock (SVB) caused a massive repricing of policy expectations and a spike in volatility.

claims.speaker: Jordan Brooks
claims.quote: as periods of high macro uncertainty often correspond to periods of surprisingly high inflation or surprisingly weak growth, equity markets have tended to do poorly when macro uncertainty is elevated.
claims.claim: High uncertainty periods coincide with inflation and growth surprises that hurt equities, so equities underperform when uncertainty is high.

claims.speaker: Jordan Brooks
claims.quote: stocks were negative in both the 1970s (stagflation) and the 2000s (tech bust and global financial crisis).
claims.claim: Traditional asset Sharpe ratios swing by decade with the macro environment; stocks had negative decade excess returns in the 1970s and 2000s.

claims.speaker: Jordan Brooks
claims.quote: High macro uncertainty means we are especially unsure as to which economic environment we will end up in.
claims.claim: With high uncertainty, both a stagflation redux and a 1990s-style productivity boom are plausible, so a single-asset bet is riskier than usual.

claims.speaker: Jordan Brooks
claims.quote: Bonds and commodities in a strategic allocation can help mitigate poor equity market performance due to negative growth shocks (bonds) or positive inflation shocks (commodities).
claims.claim: Bonds hedge negative growth shocks and commodities hedge positive inflation shocks, so adding both reduces dependence on equities.
claims.direction: hold bonds and commodities alongside equities

claims.speaker: Jordan Brooks
claims.quote: a simple “risk parity” portfolio in which the weight on each asset class is inversely proportional to its realized volatility
claims.claim: The equal-risk portfolio weights stocks, bonds and commodities in inverse proportion to their realized volatility.
claims.exact_rule: w_i proportional to 1/realized_vol_i across {MSCI World, US Govt bonds, BCOM}; lookback and rebalancing not stated
claims.data_needed: MSCI World; Bloomberg Barclays US Govt Bond Index (Ibbotson US Intermediate Govt pre-1973); Bloomberg Commodity Index; ICE BofAML 3M T-bill

claims.speaker: Jordan Brooks
claims.quote: delivers much more consistent performance across macroeconomic environments than equities (or any single asset class).
claims.claim: The inverse-vol equal-risk portfolio had positive Sharpe in every decade and the highest full-sample Sharpe, more consistent than any single asset.
claims.reported_result: Figure 4: equal-risk Sharpe ~0.3-0.8 in every period; ~0.5 full sample 1970-2023 vs ~0.3 stocks

claims.speaker: Jordan Brooks
claims.quote: many long-short liquid alternative strategies have little sensitivity to the macroeconomic backdrop and can provide strong performance across a range of market environments.
claims.claim: Long-short liquid alternatives have low macro sensitivity and can diversify a traditional portfolio.

claims.speaker: Jordan Brooks
claims.quote: Bonds are defined as the Bloomberg Barclays U.S. Government Bond Index and, prior to 1973, the Ibbotson U.S. Intermediate Government Bond Index.
claims.claim: Data substitution: bonds use the Ibbotson US intermediate government index before 1973 and the Bloomberg Barclays US Government index after.
claims.exact_rule: Bond series = Ibbotson US Intermediate Govt (pre-1973) spliced to Bloomberg Barclays US Govt Bond Index (1973+)
claims.data_needed: Ibbotson (Morningstar); Bloomberg Barclays US Govt Bond Index

claims.speaker: Jordan Brooks
claims.quote: Stocks are defined as the MSCI World Index.
claims.claim: Stocks = MSCI World, commodities = Bloomberg Commodity Index, excess returns over ICE BofAML 3-month T-bill, data to March 31 2023.
claims.exact_rule: Excess return = index total return - ICE BofAML US 3M T-bill; stocks MSCI World; commodities BCOM
claims.data_needed: MSCI World; Bloomberg Commodity Index; ICE BofAML 3M T-bill

claims.speaker: Jordan Brooks
claims.quote: Trend-following strategies, which at their core profit from the systematic tendency of markets to gradually incorporate new information, tend to outperform when economic shocks are large and markets experience stress.
claims.claim: Trend following profits from markets slowly incorporating information, so it does best when economic shocks are large and markets are stressed.
claims.direction: long trend following in high uncertainty
claims.testable: yes - conditional trend returns on JLN

claims.speaker: Jordan Brooks
claims.quote: has posted positive returns in the three largest equity market drawdowns since the inception of the index in 2000
claims.claim: The SG Trend index (equal-weighted 10 largest trend CTAs) was positive in the three largest MSCI World drawdowns since 2000 and averaged +21.1% vs -32.1% across five drawdowns.
claims.reported_result: Figure 5 (monthly returns; read from chart): avg SG Trend +21.1% vs MSCI World -32.1%; Nov07-Feb09 ~+21% vs ~-53%; Apr00-Sep02 ~+51% vs ~-47%; Jan22-Sep22 ~+35% vs ~-25%; Jan20-Mar20 ~+2% vs ~-21%; Oct18-Dec18 ~-5% vs ~-13% (net of fees as index of managers)
claims.indicator: SG Trend Index vs MSCI World drawdowns
claims.conditions: fails in short sharp drawdowns (Oct-Dec 2018 negative, Q1 2020 ~flat)

claims.speaker: Jordan Brooks
claims.quote: may provide even more robust tail protection, as well as superior average returns.
claims.claim: Adding economic trends (Brooks et al 2023) and alternative markets (Babu et al 2020) to price trend may improve both tail protection and average return.
claims.indicator: economic trend following; trends in alternative markets

claims.speaker: Jordan Brooks
claims.quote: the abundance of economic catalysts and cross-market dispersion associated high macro uncertainty can make the opportunity set more attractive for some strategies.
claims.claim: High macro uncertainty brings more catalysts and cross-market dispersion, improving the opportunity set for some global macro strategies.
claims.testable: partly - macro strategy returns vs JLN

claims.speaker: Jordan Brooks
claims.quote: Brooks (2017) presents a systematic approach to global macro investing that has historically delivered attractive and positively convex returns.
claims.claim: The cited macro momentum strategy (Brooks 2017) delivered attractive, positively convex returns historically.

claims.speaker: Jordan Brooks
claims.quote: Admittedly, we’d recommend this kind of diversification unconditionally.
claims.claim: Diversification into bonds, commodities, trend and alternatives is recommended at all times, not only when uncertainty is high.

claims.speaker: Jordan Brooks
claims.quote: Timing when you need diversification is a fool’s errand
claims.claim: Trying to time diversifiers fails because investors tend to add them too late.
claims.testable: partly - timing rules can be backtested

claims.speaker: AQR
claims.quote: This material is not research and should not be treated as research.
claims.claim: Standard AQR disclosures: not research or advice, past performance not indicative, forecasts may change; index returns unmanaged and gross of fees.

claims.speaker: AQR
claims.quote: The AQR Funds - AQR Managed Futures Strategy Fund is a constituent of the SG Trend Index.
claims.claim: The author firm manages a fund inside the SG Trend Index used as evidence, a potential conflict of interest.

reasoning.question: Is the high macroeconomic uncertainty of 2020-23 likely to persist rather than revert to the calm 2010s, and what should investors hold if it does? It matters because high uncertainty coincides with high equity volatility and poor equity returns.

thesis.statement: Macro uncertainty is highly persistent statistically and is reinforced by central-bank trade-offs and market/forecaster disagreement, so it will likely stay high; investors should diversify away from equity risk into bonds, commodities, risk parity, trend following and macro strategies.

foundations.premise: Uncertainty can be measured as the volatility of forecast errors of macro data (JLN).
foundations.support: JLN 2015 methodology; cross-check with a simple forecast-error index (corr 0.7)

foundations.premise: Volatility-type quantities are persistent and therefore forecastable, unlike returns.
foundations.support: analogy to stock volatility; AR(1) on JLN

foundations.premise: Monetary policy acts with long and variable lags via rate-sensitive demand and bank credit.
Central banks effectively have a dual mandate, so inflation-employment trade-offs create policy uncertainty.
Disagreement between prices and forecasts must resolve, and resolution produces volatility.
foundations.support: logic only; no historical test of the disagreement measure

foundations.premise: Markets incorporate new information gradually, which is why trend following works.
foundations.support: assertion plus SG Trend drawdown evidence and AQR citations

mechanism_chain.to: lagged slowdown while inflation still above target (trade-off)
mechanism_chain.why: long and variable lags; policy works through rate-sensitive demand and bank credit
abrupt policy reversals and unclear policy path

mechanism_chain.from: market pricing vs forecaster disagreement (rates, inflation, across assets)
mechanism_chain.why: either markets reprice or Fed credibility erodes

mechanism_chain.to: high and persistent market volatility and weak equities
mechanism_chain.why: uncertainty coincides with inflation/growth surprises; JLN co-moves with VIX

mechanism_chain.from: persistent uncertainty about which regime arrives
mechanism_chain.to: diversify: bonds (growth shocks), commodities (inflation shocks), risk parity, trend, macro
mechanism_chain.why: each diversifier pays off in a different regime; trend gains from large shocks

design_rationale.choice: Use JLN (conditional vol of forecast errors, 132 series) as the uncertainty measure
design_rationale.reason_given: more theoretically appealing (expected not realized errors) and broader data
design_rationale.alternatives: simple average absolute forecast error of GDP, CPI, IP
design_rationale.sensitivity: corr 0.7 with the simple measure; results with it not shown

design_rationale.choice: AR(1) without constant to forecast JLN
design_rationale.reason_given: persistence is the key feature; simple model

design_rationale.choice: Trade-off months: core PCE > 4% and unemployment > CBO NAIRU
Equal-risk portfolio with inverse realized-vol weights
design_rationale.reason_given: simple risk parity to show consistency across regimes

design_rationale.choice: Splice Ibbotson intermediate govt bonds before 1973

evidence_map.rules_out: rapid mean reversion to 2010s levels under a stable AR(1)
evidence_map.does_not_rule_out: (reader) regime shifts; JLN is itself a smoothed conditional-volatility estimate, which mechanically raises persistence
evidence_map.strength: moderate - strong persistence but model is trivially simple and in-sample

evidence_map.result: JLN averages 0.6 in trade-off months vs -0.1 otherwise, t > 7
evidence_map.does_not_rule_out: (reader) trade-off months are few and clustered (1970s-early 80s, 2022), so effective sample is tiny and the t-stat ignores autocorrelation; causality may run from shocks to both

evidence_map.result: JLN > 1 months: equities -16% vs +6%; vol 21% vs 12%
evidence_map.rules_out: no relation between uncertainty and equity outcomes
evidence_map.does_not_rule_out: (reader) contemporaneous only; equity crashes may raise JLN rather than JLN predicting returns

evidence_map.result: JLN corr 0.6 with VIX, 0.5 with realized vol
SG Trend positive in 3 largest equity drawdowns since 2000, avg +21.1% vs -32.1%
evidence_map.does_not_rule_out: (reader) 5 hand-picked episodes; no direct test of trend returns conditional on JLN
evidence_map.strength: weak - small sample, not linked to the uncertainty measure

evidence_map.result: Decade Sharpe ratios vary widely; equal risk more consistent

regimes.condition: Fed trade-off (core PCE > 4% and unemployment > NAIRU)

regimes.effect: trend following gave little or negative protection

gaps_and_conflicts.issue: Stated AR coefficient 0.98 implies a half-life of ~2.9 years and a one-year forecast of ~1.0 from 1.27; the stated ~4-year half-life and 1.06/0.89 forecasts imply an unrounded coefficient near 0.985
t-stat > 7 likely ignores strong autocorrelation of JLN (AR 0.98); HAC or block bootstrap not reported
The disagreement catalyst is argued but not tested historically (no series of SEP-futures gap vs later volatility)
Risk-parity vol lookback, rebalancing frequency and leverage unstated
US equity index used for the JLN>1 test and sample dates not specified
Author recommends diversification unconditionally yet frames it as timely now; also says timing is a fool's errand
SG Trend index contains an AQR fund (author's firm)
JLN is revised as the factor model is re-estimated; a point-in-time version is not discussed

relations.why: trend tends to profit when uncertainty and shocks are large
cited as giving more robust tail protection and convex returns
same persistence logic applied to macro uncertainty

reasoning.forward_looking_inputs: (reader) The JLN level (and its AR(1) forecast) is a months-to-years lead for equity volatility and a conditioning variable for trend/macro allocations; a Fed trade-off dummy (core PCE > 4% and unemployment > NAIRU) and the gap between SEP dots and futures-implied rates are candidate leading indicators of rate volatility over months. They would stop working if central banks regained a no-trade-off regime, if JLN mean-reverted faster than its AR(1), or if the disagreement resolved quietly.
reader_inferences: (reader) The half-life arithmetic does not match the rounded 0.98 coefficient; the true estimate is likely ~0.985.
(reader) JLN is a smoothed conditional-volatility estimate, so its persistence is partly mechanical.
(reader) The JLN>1 equity result is contemporaneous and cannot by itself be used as a timing signal.
(reader) Trade-off months cluster in few episodes, so the t > 7 overstates the evidence.
(reader) A testable rule for a macro book: scale up trend/macro allocations when JLN is high; the paper does not test this and argues against timing diversification.
